title: Open Policy Agent - Homepage
snippet: OPA is an open-source, general-purpose policy engine that decouples policy decision-making from services by providing a unified way to define and enforce rules across microservices, Kubernetes, APIs, CI/CD pipelines, and infrastructure. OPA uses a high-level declarative language called Rego to express policies. As a graduated project of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), OPA is recognized for its performance and proven support.
claim: OPA/Rego is a CNCF-graduated general-purpose policy engine for declarative rule enforcement

topic: AWS Cedar policy language for authorization

title: Cedar — Policy Language for Modern Authorization
snippet: AWS Cedar is an open-source language designed for authorization policies with deliberately constrained grammar. Cedar's design choices — default-deny, forbid-wins-over-permit, order-independent evaluation, no side effects — make policies easier to reason about compositionally. AWS shipped Cedar as the policy engine inside Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Policy in March 2026.
claim: Cedar is AWS-designed policy language for authorization with deterministic evaluation; shipped in Bedrock AgentCore in March 2026

topic: Cedar support for RBAC and ABAC patterns
query: Cedar policy language ABAC attribute based access control
title: Cedar Policy Language Reference Guide
snippet: Cedar is a simple yet expressive language designed to support common authorization use cases, such as role-based access control (RBAC) and attribute-based access control (ABAC). Cedar policies have three components: the effect (permit or forbid), the scope (constraining principal, action, and resource), and conditions (optional expressions adding further constraints based on attributes).
claim: Cedar supports RBAC, ABAC, and ReBAC patterns with condition-based attribute evaluation

topic: Policy as Code decision point architecture

title: What is Policy as Code?
snippet: Policy as Code follows the same lifecycle as application code: define, review, test, deploy, and observe. A policy decision point (PDP) is a rules or policy engine responsible for applying policies and returning a decision on whether a particular access is permitted. The PDP allows authorization logic to be offloaded to a separate system from application code.
claim: Policy as Code uses a separate Policy Decision Point (PDP) for access decisions, following application code lifecycle

title: Policy Engine Showdown - OPA vs. OpenFGA vs. Cedar
snippet: Two main architectural patterns exist: Policy as Data stores all information needed for authorization (namespaces, relationship tuples, rules) in a centralized system with queries to a datastore; Policy as Code relies on external data sources (application databases) to provide context for access checks, with policies written in domain-specific languages allowing detailed, logic-based rules.
claim: Policy engines follow data-driven (centralized datastore) or code-driven (external data sources) architectural patterns

topic: Cedar vs Rego safety and performance comparison
query: policy engine enforcement Open Policy Agent Cedar Rego 2026
title: Security Benchmarking Authorization Policy Engines: Rego, Cedar, OpenFGA & Teleport ACD
snippet: Rego is expressive but error-prone, failing several tests due to runtime exceptions, non-determinism, and extensibility risks. Cedar is safe and deterministic, with strong validation and isolation, but less flexible for complex rules outside typical access control. Cedar's fixed grammar prevents accidental side effects and makes policies safer to compose.
claim: Cedar prioritizes safety and determinism over Rego's flexibility; Cedar passes Cedar-specific validation tests that Rego fails
